At the start of the day, 205 players out of the starting field of 1,823 entries returned to Casino Barcelona , all having secured a piece of the massive €8,841,550 prize pool. After five levels of play, only 67 of them still have a shot at becoming the newest EPT champion and banking the top prize of €1,370,050 . At the end of the night, Fabricio Nociolini bagged 2,510,000, worth 167 big blinds when play resumes on Day 4. Nociolini got the majority of his chips during the final phases of the night, starting the final level inside the top ten before hitting a two-outer to eliminate Oleg Vasylchenko and catching Jacek Skiscim with a huge bluff to end the evening with the chip lead. Second in chips is Joris Ruijs , who was the only other player to cross the two-million mark. With 2,185,000, the Dutchman is eyeing a second deep run in an EPT Main Event this year, having finished ninth at EPT Paris. Romania's Alexandru Toderita completes the top three with 1,970,000. Sebastian Malec , looking to recreate the magic on the 10th anniversary of his iconic EPT Barcelona Main Event victory, bagged 1,950,000, in large part due to Alexander Ivarsson six-betting all in with pocket eights into Malec's pocket kings during the final hands of Day 3. He too remains in contention for a historic double, bagging 990,000 for an above-average stack. Similarly, 2023 EPT Barcelona champion Simon Wiciak remains in contention, although with 415,000, he is among the shorter stacks of the field. Two other EPT winners still have a shot at claiming their second titles: 2010 EPT Grand Final champion Nicolas Chouity (1,050,000), and Mark Teltscher (695,000), who won EPT London all the way back in 2005. On the flip side, EPT champions Anton Wigg (189th - €9,900) and Barny Boatman (182nd - €11,400) saw their runs come to an end during the early stages of Day 3. They were joined on the rail by the likes of Leo Worthington-Leese (134th - €13,100), Parker Talbot (128th - €13,100), Andrea Dato (101st - €15,050), Alexandre Reard (99th - €15,050), Ankit Ahuja (98th - €15,050), and Nacho Barbero (69th - €19,900). Meanwhile, one of the many interesting storylines reached its conclusion on Day 3, as Ireland's John Dwyer finished 105th for €15,050 for his first-ever EPT cash. Dwyer was one of two brothers taking their seats on Day 3, with Day 1 chip leader Michael Dwyer remaining in contention with a stack of 615,000. John Dwyer Day 4 of the EPT Barcelona Main Event will begin on Wednesday, August 26, at noon local time. The blinds will be 10,000/15,000 with a 15,000 big blind ante, and the provisional schedule calls for four 90-minute levels to be played. A short break will take place after every level, with the day scheduled to finish around 7 p.m. local time, although this may be subject to change. The 67 remaining players have all locked up €19,900 for making it this far, with a pay jump to €22,900 some ways away at 55th place. Six-figure payouts await when the field is reduced to a final table of nine players, while the top three finishers will all take home more than half a million. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/03/russ.text: Russia has the highest rate of cat ownership in the world, with nearly 59% of households keeping at least one cat — and an estimated 2.8 million stray cats living on its streets, a number that rose sharply after the 2022 mobilisation order sent thousands of pet owners fleeing the country or to the front amid Russia's ongoing all-out war in Ukraine.According to a 2024-2026 study by analytics platform Seasia Stats, Russia ranks first globally for cats as pets. Romania ranks second in Europe at 48%, followed by Poland at 41%, Latvia at 37% and Hungary at 35%.Outside Europe, Indonesia, the Philippines, Thailand, New Zealand and the US also make the top 10. The Seasia Stats findings are consistent with a 2023 study by insurer Ingosstrakh and the Financial University, in which 58.8% of Russian respondents described themselves as cat owners.The stray figures come from a separate study by the Centre for Animal Nutrition and Well-being Studies, the Nika animal charity and research firm Ipsos.They put the total stray animal population in Russia in 2025 at nearly 3.6 million, of which 2.8 million are cats and 800,000 are dogs.Of those, around 170,000 were in shelters at the time of the study, while the rest were living on the streets. Researchers say up to 98% of stray cats and dogs were once domestic pets abandoned by their owners.Animal welfare organisations recorded a sharp increase in abandonments after Russia announced partial mobilisation in September 2022.Men who received call-up papers were either leaving the country or preparing for deployment and in many cases could not arrange care for their animals or find shelter places.On classified advertising websites, owners threatened to have pets put down if no one took them. Shelter volunteers reported similar ultimatums from people surrendering animals in person.Russia has 819 shelters, the overwhelming majority privately run, alongside hundreds of charities and tens of thousands of volunteers. Together they care for between 170,000 and 250,000 animals — no more than 5–7% of the estimated stray population.The popularity of cats in Eastern Europe has historical roots: before industrialised agriculture, cats served a practical function on farms, where their presence and scent deterred rodents.In Southeast Asia, researchers link rising ownership to urbanisation and the growth of a middle class.Cats have lived alongside humans for around 10,000 years. Today, they are human companions of choice, alongside dogs.

https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-eyes-.text: BRUSSELS — The European Commission is exploring whether to use revenue from a global tax agreement on multinational companies to finance the EU’s next seven-year budget , four EU diplomats with knowledge of the proceedings told POLITICO. The idea could facilitate an agreement on new EU-wide taxes, known as own resources, which has emerged as a major stumbling bloc in the ongoing budget negotiations. The European Council President António Costa has urged countries to approve the new taxes to reduce national contributions to the bloc's budget, which is worth €1.82 trillion according to the latest proposal from earlier this month. Advertisement Advertisement Costa, who is brokering budget talks, is pressuring leaders to reach a budget deal among themselves by the end of the year — before elections in Poland, France and Italy threaten to derail the negotiations. Yet after more than a year of haggling, EU governments are still at odds over five proposed new taxes that the Commission estimates would generate €65 billion per year. Among the options on the table, a corporate tax known as CORE — which charges a lump sum on companies’ revenues exceeding €100 million — has emerged as the most unpopular option and is particularly toxic in Germany. To break the deadlock, French President Emmanuel Macron supported funneling part of the tax on multinationals to the EU budget during a leaders’ summit in October, said two of the diplomats. They were granted anonymity, like others, to discuss the sensitive plans. Supporters argue that this idea could garner more political support than CORE as it targets companies’ profits as opposed to their revenue. “The corporate income tax is about taxing companies based on their profitability. CORE is not about that, CORE is about taking a toll blindly,” said Pascal Saint-Amans, a former OECD official and one of the architects of the global tax arrangement. Advertisement Advertisement The tax deal Under the OECD tax deal from 2021, EU countries are compelled to levy a 15 percent minimum corporate tax on large multinationals with an annual turnover exceeding €750 million. Controversially, the U.S. secured an exemption from the rules as it introduced a national tax arrangement that was deemed equivalent to the OECD framework. The end goal is to prevent countries from competing to offer lower and lower corporate tax rates to attract large multinationals. Historically, many foreign multinationals operating across the EU such as Apple and Google have set their headquarters in Ireland because of its low taxes and light-touch regulation. To tackle this phenomenon, the OECD deal compels countries undercutting the 15 percent rate to levy a “top-up tax” on large foreign companies. Currently, the revenue is collected by national governments. However, European capitals could funnel part of these proceeds to the bloc’s budget, the diplomats said. Advertisement Advertisement This could hit countries such as Ireland and the Netherlands which charge low corporate rates and collecting large sums from the top-up tax. The Dutch government alone collected €449 million in 2026 from returns related to the global minimum tax, according to Bloomberg . Saint-Amans defended the potential new own resource on the grounds that the multinationals’ "activities are taking place in Ireland, but are about managing the EU markets." “That's how I believe that it could make sense to visualize” the top-up taxes, he added. Costa’s team and the Commission are looking into this option ahead of bilateral discussions with EU countries starting next week. Costa will test the waters with governments before proposing new budget figures and EU taxes ahead of a leaders’ summit on Nov. 26 and 27.

https://www.manilatimes.net/2026/10/30/t.text: TMT Newswire GlobeNewswire Notice of Settlement Agreement By GlobeNewswire October 30, 2026 Resize Small Medium Large Today, 30 October 2026, AS Tallinna Vesi reached out-of-court settlement with Aktsiaselts Tallinna Sadam in the water price difference dispute. The parties have entered into settlement agreement pursuant to which the claimant will withdraw their claim. This settlement follows the earlier out-of-court resolution of the disputes with Tallinn University of Technology, Aktsiaselts Olerex, EfTEN SPV2 OÜ, EfTEN Sky OÜ and Kadrioru Ärikeskus OÜ. Tallinna Vesi seeks to resolve all remaining court cases related to water price difference claims from the previous decade on similar principles. Under the agreement, Aktsiaselts Tallinna Sadam will discontinue their claim, while Tallinna Vesi will make settlement payment of €302,555, an amount broadly equivalent to 50% of the claimant’s principal claim and will reimburse the agreed ancillary costs and legal costs. According to Taavi Gröön, Chief Financial Officer of Tallinna Vesi, the settlement allows the Company to focus fully on its core activities. "We have reached agreements with a significant proportion of the claimants to resolve the disputes, and our aim is to settle the remaining court cases dating back to the previous decade. This will help avoid further years of litigation and additional costs, allowing us to focus our attention and resources on delivering an essential water service and supporting the Company’s long-term development,” said Gröön. He added that the company has always provided consumers with stable, high-quality water service. The costs associated with the settlement will be covered by provisions established in previous reporting periods.
